The metallic close-out layer is applied over a zirconia-based thermal barrier coating layer.
The close-out layer is at least 4 mils thick to ensure complete coverage.
Glass bead peening is the preferred method to densify and seal the surface of the close-out layer.
One test specimen survived 1319 thermal cycles between a burner flame and cooling air.
Another test specimen survived 3396 thermal cycles with only light oxidation observed.
The tubular stainless steel specimen with internal cooling survived over 1800 cycles at up to 1110°F (600°C).
Ni, Ni-16Cr-6Al-Y, FeCrAlSiZr, and FeCrAlY alloys were also tried for the close-out layer but had less success.
The bond coat is typically 3-7 mils thick and the ceramic thermal barrier layer is 10-30 mils thick.
Intermediate layers of mixed metal and ceramic are also possible in the coating system.
The outer surface temperature of the thermal barrier coatings is expected to be 900°F to 1300°F (480°C to 700°C).
The thermal barrier coatings have interconnected porosity to reduce thermal conductivity and increase strain tolerance.
The open porosity in the coatings can allow hot gases and corrosive condensates to enter, necessitating the close-out layer.
Plastic sealers are only effective up to about 500°F (260°C), so a metallic close-out layer is needed for higher temperatures.
The close-out layer can be graded from ceramic to metal to reduce thermal shock.
The coating system was tested in a Mach 0.3 burner rig with the specimen cycling between the flame and cooling air.
